name: Recovery and Resilience Facility
impact_assessment: none (proposal not accompanied by an impact assessment)
evidence_rating: moderate on implementation, thin on impact: detailed disbursement and audit data; GDP effects only from macro models (Commission, ECB) and early IMF analysis; no ex-post causal evaluation (due 2028)
summary: The Recovery and Resilience Facility paid out EUR 450 billion (79% of its funds) by October 2026, tied to reforms and investments that countries promised, of which about two-thirds of milestones were met. Commission models suggested it could lift EU output by up to 1.4% by 2026, while ECB staff now expect a smaller 0.4-0.9% for the euro area because of widespread delays. EU auditors warn that the fund's indicators track spending progress, not real results, so its actual impact remains unmeasured until the 2028 ex-post evaluation.

indicators.objective: Financial support for reforms and investment
indicators.indicator: Output: number of plans approved; financial contribution allocated to the plans
indicators.evidence: Measured: all 27 plans approved and repeatedly revised; by 1 October 2026 EUR 450bn disbursed (79% of the envelope: EUR 279bn grants, 78% of grant envelope; EUR 171bn loans, 80%); final payment requests worth EUR 123bn under assessment; payment deadline 31 Dec 2026.

indicators.indicator: Result: number of plans implemented / milestones and targets fulfilled
indicators.evidence: Measured: 4,082 of 5,981 milestones and targets (68%) assessed as fulfilled by 1 Oct 2026; implementation on the ground ended 31 Aug 2026. ECA found absorption delayed (EUR 213bn disbursed by end-2023; only about half of funds received had reached final recipients by Oct 2023).

indicators.indicator: Objectives set in the plans achieved due to RRF support (recovery, resilience, green and digital transition)
indicators.evidence: Only outputs measured: 14 common indicators reported by Member States (e.g. 71.3 TWh annual primary energy savings by Dec 2025), but no targets or counterfactual; ECA (SR 26/2023) concluded the framework measures implementation progress, not performance. Ex-post evaluation due 2028.

indicators.indicator: NGEU raises EU real GDP by up to 1.4% in 2026 and employment by up to 0.8% (QUEST); peak gains of about 3.5% in Spain and Bulgaria
indicators.evidence: Model-based only. NiGEM simulation in the mid-term evaluation: EU GDP 0.4% higher in 2022 and unemployment 0.2 pp lower. ECB staff later estimated a smaller euro-area effect of 0.4-0.9% of GDP by 2026 (0.8-1.2% by 2031), revised over time because of widespread delays. IMF finds a short-term demand boost in high-allocation countries. No ex-post causal estimate yet.

indicators.indicator: Lower sovereign spreads and reduced financial fragmentation through joint EU borrowing
indicators.evidence: Model and market evidence (NiGEM, IMF) indicate joint borrowing helped stabilise sovereign debt markets; not separately quantified in a causal study.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Mid-term evaluation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (Staff Working Document accompanying COM(2024) 82), SWD(2024) 70
literature.authors: European Commission
literature.title: Mid-term evaluation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (Staff Working Document accompanying COM(2024) 82)
literature.method: mid-term evaluation; QUEST and NiGEM macro-model simulations (ex-ante style)
literature.outcomes: GDP; employment; spreads; implementation
literature.headline: QUEST: NGEU could raise EU real GDP by up to 1.4% in 2026 and employment by up to 0.8%; largest gains (about 3.5%) in Spain and Bulgaria; spillovers worth a quarter to a third of the total. NiGEM: EU GDP 0.4% higher in 2022, unemployment about 0.2 pp lower. Commission stresses these are model predictions, not ex-post estimates
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's mid-term evaluation used economic models to estimate the fund could lift EU output by up to 1.4% by 2026, but says these are model forecasts, not measured effects.
literature.quality: model simulation; no counterfactual data

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Report on the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, COM(2026) 546
literature.authors: European Commission
literature.title: Report on the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility
literature.method: monitoring report (disbursements, milestones, common indicators)
literature.outcomes: absorption; milestones and targets; outputs
literature.headline: EUR 450bn (79% of envelope) disbursed by 1 Oct 2026; 4,082 of 5,981 milestones and targets fulfilled (68%); EUR 123bn final requests under assessment; common indicators lack targets and counterfactual and data cannot be audited by the Commission
literature.summary_plain: By October 2026, the EU had paid out EUR 450 billion (79% of the fund) and countries had met about two-thirds of their agreed milestones; the Commission admits its indicators cannot show what the money achieved.
literature.quality: administrative data; self-reported by Member States
literature.verified: full text read (summary, disbursement and indicator sections)

literature.citation: Bańkowski, K., Benalal, N., Bouabdallah, O., De Stefani, R., Dorrucci, E., Huber, C., Jacquinot, P., Modery, W., Nerlich, C., Rodríguez-Vives, M., Szörfi, B., Zorell, N. & Zwick, C. (2024), Four years into NextGenerationEU: what impact on the euro area economy?, ECB Occasional Paper No 362
literature.authors: Bańkowski, K., Benalal, N., Bouabdallah, O., De Stefani, R., Dorrucci, E., Huber, C., Jacquinot, P., Modery, W., Nerlich, C., Rodríguez-Vives, M., Szörfi, B., Zorell, N. & Zwick, C.
literature.title: Four years into NextGenerationEU: what impact on the euro area economy?
literature.method: macro-model simulations (several models and scenarios) plus tentative panel evidence on reforms
literature.outcomes: GDP; inflation; public debt; institutional quality
literature.direction: positive (smaller and later than first expected)
literature.headline: RRF spending and reforms could raise euro-area GDP by around 0.4-0.9% by 2026 and 0.8-1.2% by 2031 depending on capital productivity and absorption; limited inflation effect; impact shifted over time due to widespread implementation delays; tentative evidence reforms modestly improved institutional quality
literature.summary_plain: ECB staff estimate the recovery fund could raise euro-area output by 0.4-0.9% by 2026, less and later than first hoped because of widespread delays.
literature.quality: model-based; scenario range

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2024), Absorption of funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility - Progressing with delays and risks remain regarding the completion of measures and therefore the achievement of RRF objectives (Special report 13/2024), ECA Special report 13/2024
literature.authors: European Court of Auditors
literature.title: Absorption of funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility - Progressing with delays and risks remain regarding the completion of measures and therefore the achievement of RRF objectives (Special report 13/2024)
literature.method: performance audit (incl. visits to ES, IT, SK, RO)
literature.outcomes: absorption; delays; flow to final recipients
literature.headline: EUR 213bn disbursed by end-2023 (incl. EUR 56.5bn pre-financing); seven Member States had received no milestone-based payments; about half of funds received had reached final recipients by Oct 2023; delays from inflation, underestimated timelines, rule uncertainty and weak administrative capacity; disbursements do not necessarily reflect the quantity and importance of milestones achieved
literature.summary_plain: EU auditors found the recovery fund was being spent late, only about half the money paid to governments had reached final recipients by late 2023, and payments did not always match what was achieved.
literature.quality: audit

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2023), The Recovery and Resilience Facility's performance monitoring framework - Measuring implementation progress but not sufficient to capture performance (Special report 26/2023), ECA Special report 26/2023
literature.authors: European Court of Auditors
literature.title: The Recovery and Resilience Facility's performance monitoring framework - Measuring implementation progress but not sufficient to capture performance (Special report 26/2023)
literature.method: performance audit
literature.outcomes: monitoring framework
literature.headline: Milestones and targets measure implementation progress but are limited for assessing performance; common indicators give an incomplete view of outputs and results
literature.summary_plain: EU auditors concluded that for a fund billed as performance-based, the EU can track progress but cannot measure actual performance.
literature.quality: audit

literature.citation: Busse, M., Caselli, F. & Fotiou, A. (2026), The EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility: Experience and Lessons for the Next Multiannual Financial Framework, IMF Working Paper WP/26/114
literature.authors: Busse, M., Caselli, F. & Fotiou, A.
literature.title: The EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility: Experience and Lessons for the Next Multiannual Financial Framework
literature.method: sectoral and cross-country empirical analysis
literature.outcomes: output; employment; sovereign debt markets; reforms
literature.headline: Short-term demand boost supported jobs and output, especially in countries with large allocations; much growth impact still expected as absorption accelerates; joint borrowing helped stabilise sovereign debt markets; performance conditionality supported reforms in some countries; slow absorption remains a constraint
literature.summary_plain: IMF economists find the fund gave a short-term boost to jobs and output in countries that received most, and calmed debt markets, but slow spending limits its impact so far.
literature.quality: empirical, early; identification details not verified

literature.citation: Pfeiffer, P., Varga, J. & in 't Veld, J. (2022), Quantifying spillovers of coordinated investment stimulus in the EU, Macroeconomic Dynamics 27: 1843-1865
literature.authors: Pfeiffer, P., Varga, J. & in 't Veld, J.
literature.title: Quantifying spillovers of coordinated investment stimulus in the EU
literature.method: DSGE model simulation (QUEST)
literature.outcomes: GDP; cross-border spillovers
literature.headline: Basis of the Commission's NGEU estimates: coordinated investment across Member States generates substantial positive cross-border spillovers
literature.summary_plain: Commission economists' model showing that spending the recovery funds at the same time in all countries amplifies the boost to growth through cross-border spillovers.
literature.quality: model; authors are Commission staff
literature.verified: page summary via search (bibliographic data via Crossref)
literature.interested_party: Authors are European Commission (DG ECFIN) staff

literature.authors: Di Pietro, F., Haustein, E., Conte, A., D'Adamo, G. & Winterhager, V.
literature.title: EU Budget: The crowd-in effects
literature.venue: JRC Working Papers on Territorial Modelling and Analysis 2026-06
literature.method: synthetic control (country-level) for the RRF; local projections for ESIF
literature.outcomes: total, public and private investment (capital formation)
literature.headline: Synthetic control shows a positive and increasing effect of the RRF on total investment from 2022 onward, driven mainly by private investment (abstract gives no point estimate).
literature.summary_plain: EU recovery money appears to have raised investment in recipient countries, and most of the extra investment came from private firms rather than governments.
literature.quality: Causal design (synthetic control), but few treated units and the RRF hit all EU states at once, so donor pool and timing are hard; Commission in-house research.
literature.interested_party: European Commission (JRC) evaluating an EU instrument
literature.citation: Di Pietro, F., Haustein, E., Conte, A., D'Adamo, G. & Winterhager, V. (2026), EU Budget: The crowd-in effects, JRC Working Papers on Territorial Modelling and Analysis 2026-06

literature.authors: Zorell, N. & Zwick, C.
literature.title: Assessing the impact of the EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility on institutional quality: a Bayesian synthetic control approach
literature.method: Bayesian synthetic control on Worldwide Governance Indicators, data to 2024
literature.outcomes: institutional quality (WGI)
literature.headline: Finds robust, economically meaningful RRF-induced improvements in institutional quality in Italy; evidence for other main beneficiaries ranges from suggestive to limited.
literature.summary_plain: The recovery fund seems to have improved the quality of government institutions in Italy, but the evidence for other big recipient countries is weak.
literature.period_geography: Italy, Spain, other main RRF beneficiaries; 2021-2024
literature.quality: Causal design but country-level, short post-period, and WGI are perception-based indicators; authors say too early for firm conclusions.
literature.citation: Zorell, N. & Zwick, C. (2026), Assessing the impact of the EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility on institutional quality: a Bayesian synthetic control approach, ECB Working Paper Series No 3212

literature.authors: Accetturo, A., Baltrunaite, A., Lazzaro, E. & Mancini, A. L.
literature.title: Do Incentives and Organizational Innovations Affect the Performance of Public Administrations? Lessons from the Italian NRRP
literature.method: within- and across-municipality variation in NRRP-funded vs other public works contracts (difference-in-differences-type design)
literature.outcomes: speed of procurement awarding, start and progress of works
literature.headline: The NRRP significantly improved procurement awarding and higher upfront liquidity sped the start of works, but no appreciable effect on the subsequent progress of works.
literature.summary_plain: Italy's recovery plan made town halls quicker at awarding public works contracts and starting construction, but did not make the building itself go faster.
literature.quality: Credible quasi-experimental design on administrative contract data; authors are Bank of Italy economists; single country.
literature.citation: Accetturo, A., Baltrunaite, A., Lazzaro, E. & Mancini, A. L. (2026), Do Incentives and Organizational Innovations Affect the Performance of Public Administrations? Lessons from the Italian NRRP, CEPR Discussion Paper 21596

literature.authors: Ferri, G., Menghini, M. & Pini, M.
literature.title: Does the NRRP speed up firms' Twin Transition? Empirical evidence from Italy
literature.method: firm survey of almost 3,000 Italian firms; probit-type regressions with instrumental-variables robustness
literature.outcomes: firm green and digital (twin transition) investment; firm performance
literature.headline: Firms activating NRRP projects are more likely to start and to continue twin-transition investment, especially in disadvantaged segments and areas; results robust to IV.
literature.summary_plain: Italian firms that took part in recovery-plan projects were more likely to invest in going green and digital.
literature.quality: Survey-based and early; selection into NRRP projects is a concern despite IV; one co-author is from the Italian Treasury.
literature.citation: Ferri, G., Menghini, M. & Pini, M. (2023), Does the NRRP speed up firms' Twin Transition? Empirical evidence from Italy, Working paper (MEF / CEIS Tor Vergata)

literature.authors: Fernández Cerezo, A., Puente Díaz, S. & Veiga Duarte, R.
literature.title: Weak business investment in Spain following the pandemic: an analysis based on the Banco de España Business Activity Survey
literature.method: special module of the Banco de España Business Activity Survey (EBAE), descriptive statistics
literature.outcomes: additionality of NGEU-funded firm investment
literature.headline: 45% of firms with NGEU-funded projects said they would not have made the investments without the funds and 31% would have made only part of them; additionality lower for green investment.
literature.summary_plain: Most Spanish firms that got EU recovery money say they would not have invested as much without it, though the effect is weaker for green projects.
literature.quality: Self-reported counterfactual from firms, not a causal estimate; large representative central-bank survey.
literature.citation: Fernández Cerezo, A., Puente Díaz, S. & Veiga Duarte, R. (2025), Weak business investment in Spain following the pandemic: an analysis based on the Banco de España Business Activity Survey, Banco de España Economic Bulletin 2025/Q1

literature.authors: Havlik, A., Heinemann, F., Helbig, S. & Nover, J.
literature.title: Dispelling the shadow of fiscal dominance? Fiscal and monetary announcement effects for euro area sovereign spreads in the corona pandemic
literature.method: event study regressions on government bond spreads of ten euro countries
literature.outcomes: sovereign bond spreads
literature.headline: Only the Next Generation EU announcement among fiscal measures had a smaller but statistically significant spread-reducing effect; PEPP had much larger effects.
literature.summary_plain: Announcing the EU recovery fund (of which the RRF is the core) slightly lowered borrowing costs for weaker euro countries, though ECB bond buying mattered far more.
literature.quality: Clean high-frequency event study, but measures the NGEU announcement (before the RRF Regulation), not the Regulation's implementation.
literature.citation: Havlik, A., Heinemann, F., Helbig, S. & Nover, J. (2021), Dispelling the shadow of fiscal dominance? Fiscal and monetary announcement effects for euro area sovereign spreads in the corona pandemic, ZEW Discussion Paper 21-050

literature.authors: Espinosa, P.
literature.title: On the Impact of Next Generation EU Funds: A Regional Synthetic Control Method Approach
literature.method: regional synthetic control (Spanish regions)
literature.outcomes: regional GDP per capita
literature.headline: Finds NGEU funds raised Spanish regional GDP per capita in 2022 relative to a no-NGEU counterfactual (abstract gives no magnitude; 2023-24 projected).
literature.summary_plain: Spanish regions appear to have grown a little faster in 2022 because of EU recovery funds.
literature.quality: Weak: unclear donor pool (all EU regions treated), very early and partly projected; unpublished working paper; author flags caution.
literature.citation: Espinosa, P. (2023), On the Impact of Next Generation EU Funds: A Regional Synthetic Control Method Approach, Universitat de València Working Papers

literature.authors: European Court of Auditors
literature.title: Support from the Recovery and Resilience Facility for the digital transition in EU member states (Special report 13/2025)
literature.method: performance audit: document review, surveys of member states, sample of 27 digital measures in DK, FR, IT, LU, RO; milestone completion analysis
literature.outcomes: digital spending allocation, milestones and targets, results of digital measures
literature.headline: All member states met the 20% digital spending target, but more than one third of final milestones and targets in the sample were inadequate or unambitious and results could be assessed for only 5 of 15 completed measures; a 'missed opportunity'.
literature.summary_plain: Auditors found countries met the rule to spend a fifth of recovery money on digital, but often not on their biggest digital weaknesses, and progress is poorly measured.
literature.quality: Independent audit with structured sample; qualitative-plus-counts, not causal.
literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2025), Support from the Recovery and Resilience Facility for the digital transition in EU member states (Special report 13/2025), European Court of Auditors

literature.authors: European Court of Auditors
literature.title: RRF support for an improved business environment (Special report 21/2025)
literature.method: performance audit of business-environment reforms across all RRPs and 25 sampled reforms in BG, ES, CY, AT
literature.outcomes: coverage of country-specific recommendations; outputs and results of reforms
literature.headline: Two thirds of 2019-2020 business-environment sub-CSRs were addressed by RRPs, but almost half only marginally and none in full; only one third of completed sampled reforms showed significant results.
literature.summary_plain: The recovery fund's business reforms tackled some of the EU's recommendations, but rarely fully, and only a third of finished reforms showed real results.
literature.period_geography: EU-27; BG, ES, CY, AT; Feb 2020-Apr 2025
literature.quality: Independent audit; structured assessment with counts; small reform sample.
literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2025), RRF support for an improved business environment (Special report 21/2025), European Court of Auditors

literature.authors: Darvas, Z., Welslau, L. & Zettelmeyer, J.
literature.title: The EU Recovery and Resilience Facility falls short against performance-based funding standards
literature.method: structured content analysis of milestones and targets in seven national recovery plans (input/output/result classification)
literature.outcomes: use of result vs input/output indicators in national plans
literature.headline: Input indicators make up more than half of all indicators for Germany, almost half for France and over a third for the Netherlands and Spain, while Finland, Italy and Romania use many result indicators.
literature.summary_plain: Bruegel found that many recovery plans pay out for money spent or things built rather than for real results, which undercuts the claim that the fund is performance-based.
literature.period_geography: DE, FR, ES, FI, IT, NL, RO; plans as adopted 2021-2022
literature.quality: Descriptive design analysis of plans, not of outcomes; early.
literature.interested_party: Bruegel is funded partly by EU member states and corporate members; no specific position on the RRF
literature.citation: Darvas, Z., Welslau, L. & Zettelmeyer, J. (2023), The EU Recovery and Resilience Facility falls short against performance-based funding standards, Bruegel Analysis 08/2023

literature.authors: Ecorys, CEPS, CSIL, NIESR & Wavestone (for DG ECFIN)
literature.title: Study supporting the mid-term evaluation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility
literature.method: mixed-method evaluation: interviews and surveys of national coordination bodies, case studies, macro-model (NiGEM) estimates
literature.outcomes: GDP, unemployment, implementation, efficiency
literature.headline: Estimates GDP 0.4% higher in 2022 and unemployment 0.2 pp lower than without RRF spending; flags implementation delays and administrative burden.
literature.summary_plain: An independent consortium hired by the Commission judged that the recovery fund lifted EU output a little in 2022 but faced delays and red tape.
literature.quality: Macro effect is model-based, not estimated from outcome data; underpins the Commission's own mid-term evaluation SWD (already listed), so partly overlapping; commissioned by the Commission.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission (DG ECFIN)
literature.citation: Ecorys, CEPS, CSIL, NIESR & Wavestone (for DG ECFIN) (2024), Study supporting the mid-term evaluation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, European Commission (DG ECFIN) external study

literature.authors: Samuel De Lemos, Giacomo Loi, Mentor Mehmedi, Rudi Becker Đuricic (EGOV), Andras Schwarcz, Anda-Diana Ghiran-Merveille, Ludovica Munari (BSU), European Parliament
literature.title: Recovery and Resilience Dialogue with the European Commission: BUDG-ECON Committee meeting on 9 February 2026 (In-depth analysis, PE 779.862)
literature.venue: European Parliament, Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV) and Budgetary Support Unit
literature.method: descriptive statistics from the Commission's RRF Scoreboard (absorption, milestones, plan revisions) plus country case notes
literature.outcomes: disbursement and absorption rates, milestone fulfilment, reasons for plan amendments
literature.headline: By end-January 2026, 66% of RRF grants and 77% of loans had been disbursed, but cutting eight countries' loan envelopes alone raised the Facility-wide absorption rate from 60.5% to 68.3%, and 57% of plan amendments since June 2025 cited 'administrative simplification' (vs 15% before).
literature.summary_plain: Parliament's own analysts show that much of the recent 'progress' in spending EU recovery money comes from countries shrinking the loans they asked for, not from faster delivery, and that late plan changes increasingly water down commitments.
literature.quality: Official descriptive monitoring based on public Scoreboard data; no causal analysis; useful decomposition of absorption figures.
literature.citation: Samuel De Lemos, Giacomo Loi, Mentor Mehmedi, Rudi Becker Đuricic (EGOV), Andras Schwarcz, Anda-Diana Ghiran-Merveille, Ludovica Munari (BSU), European Parliament (2026), Recovery and Resilience Dialogue with the European Commission: BUDG-ECON Committee meeting on 9 February 2026 (In-depth analysis, PE 779.862), European Parliament, Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV) and Budgetary Support Unit

literature.authors: Manuel Hidalgo, Jorge Galindo, Javier Martínez (EsadeEcPol)
literature.title: Evolución de los Fondos Next-Gen EU en España (EsadeEcPol Policy Brief #55)
literature.method: descriptive statistics from the EsadeEcPol NextGenEU Tracker (calls, awards and beneficiaries of Spain's recovery plan, data to 12 March 2026)
literature.outcomes: funds called vs awarded, regional and sectoral distribution, concentration of beneficiaries
literature.headline: Spain had called EUR 90.7bn in RRF grants but awarded only EUR 63.4bn by March 2026 (a EUR 27bn gap), and the top 1% of beneficiaries received 71.4% of the value awarded, with construction taking over EUR 13bn versus about EUR 1.3bn for education and health combined.
literature.summary_plain: A Spanish think tank tracking the EU recovery money finds that a large share was still not awarded months before the deadline, and that most of what was awarded went to a small number of big recipients and to building works rather than skills or health.
literature.quality: Careful administrative-data tracker; descriptive only; awards are not the same as spending or impact.
literature.citation: Manuel Hidalgo, Jorge Galindo, Javier Martínez (EsadeEcPol) (2026), Evolución de los Fondos Next-Gen EU en España (EsadeEcPol Policy Brief #55), EsadeEcPol (Esade Center for Economic Policy)

literature.authors: Área financiera y digitalización de Funcas
literature.title: Fondos NextGen: ¿la transformación que no llega? (Cuadernos de Información Económica, n.º 308)
literature.method: descriptive analysis of budget execution data for Spain's Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan
literature.outcomes: commitments vs actual payments, share of current vs investment spending
literature.headline: By mid-2025 fewer than one third of Spain's NextGen budget credits had turned into actual payments, and about 25% of resources went to current rather than investment spending.
literature.summary_plain: Spain was quick to sign up for and receive EU recovery money, but slow to actually spend it, and a quarter went on day-to-day costs rather than long-term investment, so the promised transformation of the economy has been limited.
literature.quality: Descriptive budget-execution analysis by an established think tank; abstract and introduction read; no counterfactual.
literature.interested_party: Funcas is the research foundation of the Spanish savings-bank confederation (CECA)
literature.citation: Área financiera y digitalización de Funcas (2025), Fondos NextGen: ¿la transformación que no llega? (Cuadernos de Información Económica, n.º 308), Funcas, Cuadernos de Información Económica 308 (September-October 2025)
